passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position in the common law of contracts, serving as both a corrective instrument and a source of considerable doctrinal confusion. At its core, the doctrine holds that a party who makes a clear and unambiguous promise, upon which another party reasonably relies to their detriment, may be prevented from denying the enforceability of that promise even in the absence of formal consideration. The doctrine thus operates as an exception to the classical requirement that a binding contract must be supported by bargained-for consideration — an exchange of value between the parties. Courts in England and the United States have invoked promissory estoppel with some regularity since the mid-twentieth century, yet the precise contours of the doctrine remain contested, and its application has produced outcomes that are difficult to reconcile.

The difficulty stems in part from ambiguity in the doctrine's foundational requirement: that the promisee's reliance must be "reasonable." Courts have interpreted reasonableness inconsistently, particularly in commercial contexts. In a 1967 case in New York, a supplier who had orally promised to maintain a fixed price for a period of one year was held bound by that promise when the buyer demonstrably restructured its operations in anticipation of stable input costs. The court reasoned that any commercially sophisticated party would foresee such reliance. Yet in a 1971 English case involving nearly identical facts, the court declined to apply estoppel on the ground that, without a written memorandum, the alleged promise was insufficiently certain to justify the plaintiff's reliance. The divergence illustrates a deeper tension: courts have never fully agreed on whether promissory estoppel is an independent cause of action or merely a defensive shield, a distinction that bears directly on the scope and remedy available to a claimant.

Furthermore, even where courts agree that the doctrine applies, the question of remedy has proven vexing. Classical contract doctrine generally aims to place the injured party in the position they would have occupied had the contract been performed — the so-called "expectation interest." Promissory estoppel, by contrast, is typically said to protect only the "reliance interest": the expenditures or opportunities foregone by the promisee in consequence of the promise. In practice, however, courts have sometimes awarded expectation damages in estoppel cases, blurring the doctrinal boundary and generating uncertainty about whether promissory estoppel has quietly evolved into a full substitute for formal contract. Such an evolution would not be without practical merit — it would extend contractual protection to parties who, for reasons of sophistication or resources, are unable to insist on written agreements. Regrettably, however, the case law has developed haphazardly, leaving commercial parties without reliable guidance on when reliance will be protected and to what extent.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should be formally codified as an independent cause of action so that commercial parties can rely on it with confidence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although promissory estoppel was designed to correct injustices arising from broken promises, courts in England and the United States have applied it in incompatible ways.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel remains doctrinally unsettled, with inconsistent judicial interpretations of its key requirements and remedies leaving commercial parties without adequate guidance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The distinction between the expectation interest and the reliance interest is the primary source of confusion in the law of promissory estoppel.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts have quietly transformed promissory estoppel into a full substitute for formal contract, a development that, while practically beneficial, has eroded the consideration doctrine.

explanations.correct: The passage surveys the doctrine's ambiguous foundational requirement (reasonableness), its contested status as cause of action versus defense, and the remedial confusion between reliance and expectation damages — all pointing to doctrinal unsettlement that leaves parties without guidance. C integrates all three strands.
explanations.A: A prescriptive recommendation that the author hints at but never makes the central claim; this is a proposed solution, not the thesis.
explanations.B: Partially accurate but too narrow — the passage is about more than a U.S./England divergence; it addresses structural doctrinal problems throughout.
explanations.D: Too narrow — the passage identifies multiple sources of confusion, not just the expectation/reliance distinction.
explanations.E: Overstates the author's position; the author says courts 'sometimes' award expectation damages and asks whether this 'has quietly evolved,' not that the transformation is complete.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the current state of promissory estoppel doctrine can best be described as one of

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement of the doctrine's flexibility and case-by-case adaptability.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured criticism of the doctrine's haphazard development and the uncertainty it produces for commercial parties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: outright hostility toward the doctrine's deviation from the classical consideration requirement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: cautious optimism that recent decisions reconciling expectation and reliance damages will soon resolve the doctrinal confusion.

choices.label: E
choices.text: neutral description of competing judicial approaches without expressing any evaluative stance.

explanations.correct: The author uses phrases such as 'uneasy position,' 'difficult to reconcile,' 'vexing,' and 'Regrettably, however, the case law has developed haphazardly' — all signaling critical but measured dissatisfaction, not outright hostility. B captures both the valence and the restrained register.
explanations.A: The opposite of what the author signals; the passage describes the flexibility as a source of confusion, not a virtue to endorse.
explanations.C: Too strong — the author acknowledges the doctrine has 'practical merit' and does not call for its abolition.
explanations.D: Unsupported — the passage identifies no recent reconciling decisions and expresses no optimism about resolution.
explanations.E: The author clearly editorializes ('Regrettably,' 'haphazardly'), ruling out a neutral stance.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The passage introduces a legal doctrine, traces its historical development from the nineteenth century to the present, and concludes by endorsing a proposed reform.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The passage identifies a doctrinal tension, illustrates it with two contrasting judicial decisions, broadens to a second area of uncertainty, and closes with a critical assessment of the doctrine's overall state.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The passage presents a legal debate between two schools of thought, recounts the arguments of each in turn, and then proposes a synthesis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The passage defines a doctrine, gives a single illustrative case, and then argues that the case was wrongly decided.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The passage compares the doctrine of promissory estoppel to the doctrine of consideration and argues that the former has supplanted the latter in modern courts.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces the doctrine and its doctrinal tension (exception to consideration). Paragraph 2 illustrates with the 1967 New York and 1971 English cases to show inconsistent application of the 'reasonableness' requirement. Paragraph 3 turns to the second area of uncertainty — reliance versus expectation remedy — and closes with a critical assessment. B matches this four-move structure precisely.
explanations.A: The passage does not trace a historical development from the nineteenth century, nor does it endorse a specific reform.
explanations.C: The passage does not frame two 'schools of thought' or propose a synthesis; it surveys judicial inconsistency.
explanations.D: Two contrasting cases are cited, not one, and the author does not argue either was wrongly decided outright.
explanations.E: The passage raises the possibility that estoppel is evolving into a contract substitute but does not argue it has supplanted consideration.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the classical doctrine of contract law requires which one of the following for a promise to be legally binding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A written memorandum signed by both parties.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Proof that the promisee suffered a financial loss as a result of relying on the promise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bargained-for consideration constituting an exchange of value between the parties.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Evidence that the promisor was commercially sophisticated and aware of the consequences of the promise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court ruling confirming that the promisee's reliance was reasonable under the circumstances.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly states that 'a binding contract must be supported by bargained-for consideration — an exchange of value between the parties.' C is a direct paraphrase.
explanations.A: The written-memorandum requirement is mentioned in connection with the 1971 English case, not as a general requirement of classical contract law.
explanations.B: Financial loss from reliance is associated with promissory estoppel, not the classical consideration requirement.
explanations.D: Commercial sophistication is mentioned as a factor in the 1967 New York court's reasoning, not as a classical contract requirement.
explanations.E: Reasonable reliance is a requirement of promissory estoppel, not of classical contract formation.

questions.questionStem: The passage indicates that the 1967 New York court's conclusion that the supplier was bound by its oral price promise was based primarily on which one of the following considerations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The buyer had submitted a signed written document confirming its reliance on the promised price.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The supplier's promise was part of a formally negotiated commercial agreement supported by consideration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A commercially sophisticated party in the supplier's position would have anticipated that the buyer would restructure its operations in response to the promise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The buyer had no alternative suppliers available and therefore had no choice but to rely on the promise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Binding oral promises are presumed enforceable under New York commercial law regardless of reliance.

explanations.correct: The passage states that 'the court reasoned that any commercially sophisticated party would foresee such reliance,' referring to the buyer's restructuring of operations. C accurately paraphrases this reasoning.
explanations.A: No written document is mentioned in connection with the New York case; it was an oral promise.
explanations.B: The passage describes the promise as oral and lacking formal consideration — that is precisely why estoppel was required.
explanations.D: No mention is made of the buyer's access to alternative suppliers.
explanations.E: The passage does not state any presumption of enforceability for oral promises under New York law.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would most likely agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Courts should uniformly abandon promissory estoppel and return to the classical consideration requirement in all commercial disputes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The extension of promissory estoppel to award expectation damages would be of particular benefit to parties who lack the resources or sophistication to secure written agreements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 1971 English court's refusal to apply estoppel was correct because certainty of promise is the most important prerequisite for the doctrine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The distinction between promissory estoppel as a cause of action and as a defensive shield has no practical consequence for the relief a claimant may seek.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All oral commercial promises should be legally enforceable without any showing of reliance, because the certainty requirement imposes too heavy a burden on unsophisticated parties.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly states that extending estoppel into a full contract substitute 'would not be without practical merit — it would extend contractual protection to parties who, for reasons of sophistication or resources, are unable to insist on written agreements.' The author presents this as a point in favor of the evolution, supporting inference B.
explanations.A: The author does not call for abandonment of estoppel; on the contrary, the doctrine's 'practical merit' is acknowledged.
explanations.C: The author presents the 1971 English case as an example of divergence, not as the correct outcome; calling it correct would contradict the passage's critical tone.
explanations.D: The passage says the cause-of-action/defense distinction 'bears directly on the scope and remedy available,' implying practical consequence — the opposite of D.
explanations.E: The author never argues that reliance should be eliminated as a requirement; the concern is with inconsistent application of the reasonableness standard.

questions.questionStem: The author most likely discusses the contrast between the "expectation interest" and the "reliance interest" in the third paragraph primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that promissory estoppel should be limited to protecting only reliance expenditures and should never yield expectation damages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate a second dimension of doctrinal uncertainty in promissory estoppel, namely that courts have not consistently adhered to the remedy the doctrine is said to provide.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that classical contract law is superior to promissory estoppel because expectation damages more fully compensate injured parties.

choices.label: D
choices.text: explain why the 1967 New York court awarded expectation damages rather than reliance damages to the buyer.

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce the concept of consideration as the foundational principle distinguishing contract from estoppel claims.

explanations.correct: The third paragraph opens by noting that courts have 'proven vexed' by the remedy question, then shows that courts 'sometimes' award expectation damages in estoppel cases despite the doctrine's orthodox reliance-interest limitation. The function is to introduce a second, distinct area of doctrinal confusion beyond the reasonableness-of-reliance problem in paragraph 2. B captures this rhetorical purpose.
explanations.A: The author does not advocate limiting estoppel to reliance damages; the passage is descriptive and critical, not prescriptive on this point.
explanations.C: The author does not argue classical contract law is superior; the passage notes expectation damages 'blur the doctrinal boundary,' not that their availability is objectionable.
explanations.D: The 1967 New York case is discussed in paragraph 2; paragraph 3 does not revisit that case's remedy.
explanations.E: Consideration is introduced in paragraph 1; the third paragraph's function is to address remedial uncertainty, not foundational doctrine.
